newsitem.title: CUBA: U.S. embargo kept AIDS low.
newsitem.headline: U.S. embargo kept AIDS low.

text.p: A Cuban health official said on Thursday that the United States' economic embargo on the communist-ruled island had helped keep the rate of AIDS low.

Jorge Perez, deputy director of Cuba's Tropical Medicine Institute, told a conference on AIDS that the American "blockade" had ironically been a factor in helping contain the disease because of the isolation it had provided Cuba from the United States.
Cuba routinely blames Washington's 35-year-old embargo -- which includes restrictions on travel by U.S. citizens -- for economic and other woes, including problems supplying the health sector.

Perez, who also heads the country's largest sanitarium for AIDS patients at Santiago las Vegas outside Havana, spoke at the start of a week-long conference on AIDS in Cuba, Latin America and the Caribbean.

Cuba, with a population of 11 million, through last month had an accumulated total of 1,649 cases of people who have tested HIV-positive since 1985. Of those, 595 people have developed full-blown AIDS, 429 of whom have died.

Perez said Cuba's approach has included mass testing and, for the first few years, isolation at sanitariums of all people who tested positive for HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, as well as those who went on to develop the illness.

Cuba has been criticised for such interventionist methods abroad, particularly over the sanitariums. Cuba's isolation of all HIV-positive and AIDS patients ended in 1993 with the introduction of out-patient treatment, although some people are still treated at the sanitariums.

Perez said the first person to be diagnosed HIV-positive was in 1985 and was someone who had come from Mozambique, but he noted that Cuba had started to develop a preventive programme two years earlier.

In the early years of testing, Cubans who had travelled to Africa -- such as soldiers who fought in the Angolan civil war -- were among a list of special groups of citizens targeted for testing as health officials actively sought to identify people carrying the disease.

By the end of 1986, some 99 people had tested HIV-positive. Most had either been on international missions abroad or had had contact with those people, Perez said. He said Cuba does not have a significant drug abuse problem.
Cuba's target list for testing had steadily widened and by 1987 included pregnant women, people entering a hospital for surgery, those infected with a venereal disease and prisoners.

Another expert on the disease, Rigoberto Torees, told the conference that HIV-positive cases had increased sharply over the last two years, although rates still remained low. He said the increase was being seen mostly among bisexuals or homosexuals, but did not give further details.
The most cases have been detected in Havana, followed by the western and central provinces of Villa Clara, Sancti Spiritus and Pinar del Rio.
